questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: First of all, I am a China studies major who had never been to China on an extended period of time, so I greatly wanted to do that before completing my bachelor's degree. Secondly, PKU is an incredibly iconic institution here in China especially within the humanities, so coming here has been a dream.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Generally, communication with PKU has been a little difficult, however, having now been here in China for a couple of months, I think I can say that that is less of a PKU problem and more a China problem in general. Most of the time, things have worked out despite now having much information in advance, so that is good. The biggest issue I faced was that I never heard back from neither UCPH nor PKU about whether the reservation for my dorm room had gone through, so I did not know whether I had anywhere to live until the day I arrived in Beijing and could physically go to the dorm building to check, which was stressful, but luckily it all did work out.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The university had set up a room where staff and other students helped you set up your campus card, WiFi, classes, schedule, etc. a couple of days before the semester started, which was very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: In order of price, highest to lowest: You can get a single room, a single room where you share a bathroom with one, same but share a bathroom with two, and lastly a double room you share with someone and a bathroom you share with another double room.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You will not have a real kitchen, which can be annoying after a while, but the campus cafeterias are pretty decent and varied, and you can get a good meal for between 10-15 DKK. Some people get minifridges or rice cookers for their dorm, but I didn't since I was just there for one semester, and that was okay too.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The dorms have a gym you can pay for, there is a pool and you can go bowling.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very happy with my room, a single in a suite with one other flatmate sharing a bathroom. The common areas were cleaned every three days or so and the staff at the dorm were always were friendly if you needed help with anything dorm- and China-related such as receiving a package etc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The course registration process happened through a website was not the most user-friendly I have ever tried, and it didn’t help that it was all in Chinese, which, even though I could read some, wasn’t optimal for most of us international students there. Luckily I got some help on the first day and ended up getting most of the courses I wanted as a first priority.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Student assistants were there to help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I had to take six classes, and five of them were my first priority, which was nice. The sixth class I ended up taking turned out to be pretty good to.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don’t stress out too much in advance about the lack of information beforehand, most students don’t get to pick classes before their first week, and you most likely will be able to find something that will work out for you!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The courses were level-wise fairly okay to engage with, however, something that I did have to get used to was the fact that in Beijing I would have a lot more coursework during the semester other than just readings. For instance, I think that every week or so I would usually have either a paper, an essay, a presentation or something to that effect, which could at times be a little much to juggle alongside everything else. However, on the other hand, that also meant that come exam season, the score I would get on my exam would comparatively matter less to my final grade because of all the other assignments, so compared to back home in Denmark, where your grade from your final exam would be the only one to count, I stressed a lot less during finals week.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My relationship to my professors here compared to the ones back home was interesting – on the one hand, there was a clearer hierarchical different and you would always address them by the title of “professor”, on the other hand, we would have class group chats where most of the communication regarding coursework would take place, and sometimes if you hadn’t shown up for class or was late for an assignment, the professor or TA would message you directly. This took a while to get used to.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: 1. Chinese Politics and Public Policy. 2. International Security Studies. 3. Case Study and Practice of International Journalism. 4. Contemporary China. 5. Public Speaking in English. 6. AI Ethics.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all of my courses to future students, especially AI Ethics, which I thought was particularly interesting for this day and age that we’re all living in. My politics course was a good brush-up on Chinese politics, which was very useful, also it was interesting hearing about the different topics from the perspective of a Chinese professor. Same goes for the Contemporary China course. Public Speaking in English was a fantastically fun course, where we got to try our hand at news speaking from a teleprompter at the PKU TV station and go to TikTok/Douyin for a field trip. International Journalism was fine too, however, it was not so much a journalism course but more a course where it became evident that the ambition of the professor was for us to produce as many videos of our life as international students in Beijing for the university’s social media as possible. However, if you like I wanted to actually go and interview Chinese people and do your own stories, that was possible within a certain limit too. The last course, ISS, was fine too, however, it was in the evening and the material was at times a bit confusing. Luckily the professor was nice, and we also did a simulation where we tried to solve a major international conflict during the last weeks of class, which was fun.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I did not know what to write for personal spending, as it would vary based on whether I went traveling or not, but a weekend trip would usually set me back around 700-1000 DKK for hotel, train and activities. Other than that, I cannot think of any costs right now that were unexpected. However, I did have to pay three months of rent + a deposit upfront at my dorm instead of simply paying by month, which is good to be aware of.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Generally food, transportation etc. in China, especially outside of major cities like Beijing and Shanghai, is relatively cheap. You can easily get a decent meal in a restaurant for about 25 DKK or less. Online shopping is also huge here, and you can often get the same things you can get at different “antique” markets for a fraction of the price there ;)

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: PKU has a great range of all different kinds of clubs, sports clubs like martial arts, basketball, tennis etc., and more culturally oriented clubs like the school choir, a Hanfu-association etc., however, most of these clubs only meet up or do activities during the weekend, which is often when many international students are out traveling. Moreover, if you don’t speak a little Mandarin, they might not let you join, because a lot of Chinese students are scared to speak English because they think their English is not good, which is a massive shame. However, I did have a friend with almost no Mandarin skills who joined two different dance groups with great success and had a blast, so it definitely is possible.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would recommend going to the club fair at the start of the semester and see whether anything catches your eye, and apart from that, I would recommend trying to sign up for as many language partner programs as you can, even if you aren’t learning Mandarin, as that can be a fun way to get to know local students. Also, if you can, sign up for the exchange student trip that the International Division plans every semester before the tickets are sold out! That was a super cool experience and a chance to see a part of China that otherwise would be hard to access as a tourist.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: This is kind of silly, but try and play Mahjong in one of the mahjong bars here and go to karaoke at least once. Its super fun, and not something you would normally do back home :)

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: You will be tempted to perhaps go traveling every weekend, and while I definitely also do recommend doing that, there is also just so much stuff to do only in Beijing that can be hard to do during the weekdays due to coursework and the fact that Beijing is huge and except for the two Summer Palaces close by, most attractions are around 30-60 minutes away by metro. Other than that, besides some of the major tourist attractions and cities around China, I can also highly recommend checking out the nearby city of Chengde (another Qing Summer Palace, not as well known, plus a full-scale copy of the Potala Palace in Tibet), as well as some of the less crowded areas of the Great Wall such as Simatai, Gubeikou (also has a water town) and Jinshanling. If you can’t figure out how to get there yourself, Beijing Hikers and Laowai在华 offer different guided tours. Also recommend trying out at least one guided tour with Beijing Postcards, the owner is a Danish guy named Lars who is a fantastically gifted storyteller and nerd of Beijing local history.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: For my own part I thought it was relatively okay, as I had been to Beijing on holiday once before and can speak the language for basic, everyday purposes. From what I’ve heard from other exchange students, it was a little more difficult because you have to set up all these different apps and VPNs and that can be a lot of work, + getting used to the speed and how everything works here practically can take some time, but after that initial adjustment period, life in China is very convenient and fun.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Apart from trying out some of the language partner exchanges, I would say just be open and take the initiative when talking to local students, but also don’t take it personally if they don’t want to have a longer relation with you. Most local students here are taking double the amount of credits international students are, and if you add the occasional language barrier on top of that, making friends with locals can be difficult, so don’t be too disappointed if it does not end up happening. If you are feeling brave, however, you can try making local friends outside of school, which I did on a trip once to Hebei province. But again, if you take the initiative and seem open and kind, then anything is possible 

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I would probably say the lack of information and the fact that relatively often professors will surprise you with an extra assignment that wasn’t on the syllabus, or some other thing that you have to do all of a sudden for some reason – things here in China move fast and change all the time, and that unpredictability can be difficult for someone like me who usually likes to map out there schedule weeks in advance. However, I think trying to be more spontaneous and just rolling with it has also been healthy for me :)

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Chinese people on the streets are very curious and friendly, and will often try and engage you in conversation (where are you from? How do you like China?). People dance in the squares at night, and if you’re feeling brave, you can join. Despite being a massively large city, Beijing also does feel at times like a small town with a tight-knit community.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1. Be open and adaptable. Things move fast in China, and sometimes you just have to adapt with it rather than get frustrated and annoyed. Things aren’t going to work out the way you might have thought, and that may be a blessing. 2. Try to learn just a little bit of Mandarin before you come here, even just a couple of phrases can be the difference between feeling constantly overwhelmed with everything and feeling like you know a bit more of what is going on. 3. While you definitely should keep in mind that the Chinese government works a lot different than the one back in Denmark, China in many ways isn’t as “scary” as it may seem from the news back home. In fact, so long as you don’t do anything outrightly stupid like you would anywhere else you travel to, it is probably one of the safest countries I’ve been to. However, you should also be aware that as a foreigner, you probably will be granted some level of privilege that local Chinese people are not, and that since PKU is one of the best universities in one of China’s richest cities, not everywhere in China is as “shiny” as there.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I cannot think of anything else right now.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I don’t even know where to start – I think just the experience of living somewhere so different as China and even so noticing all the little different things that makes all of us humans, despite where we’re from, the same. All the little experiences that makes having an everyday normal life in another country rewarding, going on a solo trip by yourself, taking to random strangers in a bar, trying out a new flavor of soda from the convenience store, meeting people from all over world and finding out how quickly lasting friendships can form.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I think it was the classic struggle of trying to balance classes, coursework, papers and trying to do a good job with all of that, with also exploring Beijing and China, making friends, both international and local, and also getting some rest every once in a while. Being on exchange can be mentally exhausting if you let yourself constantly wonder whether you’re “doing enough” – you are, and almost no matter what I promise you that you are doing better than you think :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I don’t know whether UCPH has officially renewed there exchange agreement with PKU yet or if I will be one of the last UCPH students to go here, because if so, I would like to say that that would be a massive shame. PKU is one of the best universities here in China, a country that we in Denmark need more people with proper, hands-on experience with. Despite the communication struggles, it really is a school that does a lot for its international students, and I have been given so many cool opportunities from simply just being here. It would be a great shame if future students don’t get the same chance.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
